text:
Transition counts offer a cheap complementary signal: Spotify’s [benchmark study](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) describes smoothed transition estimates and recency-weighted history aggregation. A reproducible adaptation is P(j|i)=(c_ij+λq_j)/(n_i+λ), with training-only counts and a documented prior q; this shrinks low-support rows toward the prior. Proposed fusion: s=z/T+g·log(P+ε), with bounded gate g=g_max·sigmoid(a). Initialize near the neural baseline; compare against a fixed-weight blend. This exact combination is a design proposal, not an established result. [Temperature scaling](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html) supports simple logit calibration; alone it preserves rankings, while fusion makes relative scales consequential.

For uncertainty, retain each model’s per-user hit indicator on identical users and candidates. Adapt [paired bootstrap resampling](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/) by resampling user pairs within each domain, then averaging the four domain differences equally. Report the macro HR@10 difference, its interval, and domain results. Calculated resolution: one changed hit moves domain HR by 0.005 and macro HR by 0.00125. These intervals condition on trained models and fixed candidates; they omit training-seed and candidate-sampling variability.

Keep the pinned 99-negative evaluator unchanged: [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled metrics can reverse full-catalog comparisons. Avoid interpreting sampled HR as full-catalog quality. Limit gate/calibration searches and checkpoint comparisons, log all trials, and reserve final claims for independent held-out evaluation. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) show repeated selection can overfit noisy validation estimates; ordinary paired intervals do not correct this winner-selection bias.
